attachments.fallback: Zenodo: The Metacognitive Cost: Why IQ Tests Create Barriers to Understanding Giftedness
attachments.text: IQ tests were designed to identify individuals requiring learning support, not to detect high intelligence. This paper argues that repurposing IQ tests for gifted identification creates systematic barriers. Drawing on the test-wiseness literature (Millman, Bishop, & Ebel, 1965) and research on reflective-impulsive cognitive styles (Kagan et al., 1964), we propose that IQ tests implicitly reward an impulsive response style (fast, first-interpretation) while penalizing a reflective style (deliberate, multiple-interpretation). Since cognitive style is independent of intelligence, this creates construct-irrelevant variance. Empirical findings that gifted individuals show processing speed discrepancies (Rimm et al., 2008; Lang et al., 2019) and that twice-exceptional individuals are systematically underestimated support this analysis. An autoethnographic account illustrates how reflective cognitive style manifests during WAIS-IV administration. Four experimental designs are proposed to test the hypothesis. The practical aim is to support twice-exceptional identification and to clarify that cognitive differences may exist independently of IQ scores.
attachments.title: The Metacognitive Cost: Why IQ Tests Create Barriers to Understanding Giftedness
